Machismo is a strong, often exaggerated belief that men are superior to women — and that this supposed superiority must be displayed through attitude and behavior. It is not just confidence or pride in being a man. It goes further than that. It is the idea that being a "real man" means being dominant, tough, aggressive, and in control — especially over women — and that any trait considered "weak" or "feminine" is something a man should reject, hide, or be ashamed of.

Think of it as an inflated, rigid version of masculinity that turns into an ideology — a set of unspoken rules about how a man must think, act, and present himself to the world.
What it looks like in real life

Machismo is not just an abstract idea. It shows up in real behavior, attitudes, and social norms. Here are some of the clearest signs of it:

A man with machismo might refuse to do household chores because he considers them "women's work." He may expect his partner to serve him, obey him, and not question his decisions. He may feel entitled to make all the important choices in a relationship or family without discussion. He may feel deeply insulted if a woman earns more money than him, leads a team he is on, or is publicly more successful than him — because in his worldview, that upsets the natural order.

He will almost certainly refuse to show any emotion that could be seen as weakness — no crying, no fear, no asking for help, no admitting that he is wrong. These things feel like threats to his sense of manhood. He may even respond to emotional pain with anger or aggression, because those feel more "masculine" to him.

He may also talk about women in objectifying ways, treating them as prizes, possessions, or background characters in his own story rather than as full, equal human beings.
The key ideas packed inside the word

To truly understand machismo, you need to understand the bundle of beliefs it contains. All of the following are part of it:

Male superiority. The central belief is that men are naturally stronger, more rational, more capable, and more authoritative than women. This is not seen as a preference — it is treated as a fact of life, as the natural way things should be.

Dominance and control. A man with machismo needs to feel in control — of situations, of other people, and especially of women. He may become aggressive, dismissive, or manipulative when he feels that control slipping away.

Emotional suppression. Showing vulnerability is seen as feminine, and therefore shameful. A man shaped by machismo will often bottle up his emotions or mask them with toughness, which can be deeply damaging to his own mental health and relationships.

Physical toughness. Strength, bravery, and the willingness to fight are glorified. Backing down from a confrontation, even when it is the wiser or safer choice, may feel humiliating.

Female submission. Women are expected to be gentle, obedient, domestic, and secondary. A woman who is assertive, independent, or outspoken may be seen as threatening or disrespectful.
It is both personal and cultural

This is an important distinction. Machismo is not just about individual men behaving badly. It can be woven into the fabric of an entire culture — something that a whole society reinforces without people even realizing it.

When machismo is cultural, it becomes a shared set of expectations. Boys are taught from childhood to "man up," to not cry, to be tough. Men who fail to live up to these standards may be mocked or seen as less of a man. Women may be raised to accept a submissive role as simply the way things are. Even people who privately disagree with these norms may go along with them to fit in or avoid conflict.

This is why machismo can be so persistent — it is not just one person's attitude. It is something that can get passed down through generations, embedded in language, humor, entertainment, family dynamics, workplaces, and politics.

While the word is most strongly associated with Latin American and Spanish-speaking cultures — where it originated and is most openly discussed — machismo as a phenomenon exists across cultures all over the world, under different names or no name at all.
The spectrum: from subtle to extreme

Machismo exists on a wide spectrum. At one end, it can be subtle — a man who unconsciously interrupts women in meetings, assumes he should be the one to drive, or feels slightly uncomfortable when his wife earns a promotion. He may not even realize he holds these attitudes. This subtle form is sometimes called "everyday machismo."

At the other end, machismo can be extreme and dangerous — controlling or abusive relationships, verbal aggression, physical violence, or the belief that a man has the right to "discipline" or punish women who disobey or disrespect him. In its most extreme form, machismo is closely linked to domestic violence and gender-based violence more broadly.
How it harms both women and men

The most obvious harm of machismo falls on women, who face inequality, dismissal, objectification, and in extreme cases, abuse and violence as a result of it.

But machismo also harms men, even if this is less often talked about. Men shaped by machismo are often not allowed to be fully human. They cannot grieve openly, admit fear, seek help for mental health struggles, or be seen as gentle or nurturing without facing ridicule. They are trapped inside a very narrow definition of what it means to be a man. This contributes to men suffering in silence, avoiding doctors, struggling with mental health issues, and having shallower emotional relationships.

Machismo can refer to a single person's attitude, a social behavior, or a broader cultural belief system. Here are examples of how it is used naturally in a sentence:

"His machismo wouldn't allow him to admit he was wrong, even when everyone could see it."

"She challenged the machismo of the workplace by demanding equal pay and respect."

"Growing up in that culture, he was surrounded by machismo from a very early age."

"The film explores how machismo damages not just women, but the men who feel forced to live by it."

In contemporary usage, machismo is almost always a critical term — meaning that when someone uses this word to describe a person or culture, they are pointing out a problem, not paying a compliment. It is understood today as harmful and regressive, something that holds both men and women back from living fuller, freer lives.

It is closely related to other concepts you may encounter, such as toxic masculinity (a modern term for the harmful aspects of rigid masculine norms), male chauvinism (the belief in male superiority), and patriarchy (a social system in which men hold most of the power).
If you had to sum it up: machismo is the belief that being a "real man" means being dominant, tough, and superior to women — and the set of attitudes and behaviors that flow from that belief.
